transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Mark Chen, Priya Desai, Liam O'Connor (Redwood) — Sofia Alvarez, Gabe Turner, Nadia Li (HelixCare)

[00:00] Mark Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm Mark from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me are Priya and Liam from platform/SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Sofia Alvarez: Good, thanks. excited to dig in — we want to understand how to get token-level visibility into production without killing performance.
[00:13] Gabe Turner: Yeah and also how this works inside our VPC when we go Private.
[00:18] Priya Desai: Awesome, that's exactly what we planned to cover: otel/tracing model, token-level metrics tradeoffs, span design, exporter choices, sampling strategies, and dashboards. we'll also touch on kv cache and batching metrics since you mentioned latency/throughput concerns.

[00:40] Liam O'Connor: Quick context question — are you planning to use Redwood Hosted initially or jump straight to Dedicated/Private?
[00:45] Nadia Li: We're looking at Dedicated for staging and Private for prod — data residency + regulatory reasons.
[00:50] Priya Desai: Good to know. Dedicated gives you the same runtime but fixed pools which is ideal for benchmarking token-level metrics; Private adds network/exporter placement considerations.

[01:10] Sofia Alvarez: Our key success criteria: per-token latency distribution, tail latencies per model, kv cache hit/miss rates correlated with latency, and token billing attribution. we need dashboards and traces to triage regressions.

[01:32] Mark Chen: Perfect. high level architecture we recommend: instrument at the request handler so you get a root span per inference request, then create child spans for phases: request decode, routing (model selection), batching wait, kernel execution / token generation, and post-processing. token-level metrics can be added as short-lived spans or as metric counters emitted per token.

[01:58] Gabe Turner: When you say token-level spans, do you mean one span per token? won't that be massive and blow up our tracing backend?

[02:05] Priya Desai: Exactly the concern. we typically recommend two patterns:
- token-level metrics as aggregated counters/gauges (tokens_generated_total, tokens_per_request_histogram) emitted at the end of the request; this is lightweight for metrics backends like Prometheus/OTLP metrics.
- token-level spans only for sampled requests (e.g., 0.1% of requests) for deep tracing. so you get detailed traces for a small fraction and stats for all.

[02:35] Sofia Alvarez: ok that makes sense. how about kv cache metrics? we need per-model kv cache hits/misses, average retrieval latency, and cache size per instance.

[02:45] Liam O'Connor: for kv cache we emit metrics per shard/replica: redwood.kv_cache_hits, redwood.kv_cache_misses, redwood.kv_cache_lookup_latency_seconds bucketed histogram, and redwood.kv_cache_memory_bytes. tag by model, replica_id, and region. for Private deployments you can map replica_id to host via service discovery.

[03:10] Gabe Turner: Do you expose those as Prometheus scrape endpoints or via OTLP push? we run Prometheus in our VPC and would prefer scraping for retention control.

[03:17] Priya Desai: Both are supported. for Private we recommend running an OpenTelemetry Collector in your VPC that scrapes internal Prometheus endpoints and forwards OTLP to your chosen backend, or you can host the exporter yourself. we'll share an example otel-collector.yaml. (link: https://redwood.example/docs/observability/otel-collector-sample)

[03:37] Nadia Li: any performance hit from scraping token-level counters at 15s scrape intervals?

[03:42] Priya Desai: scraping aggregates is cheap; the main overhead is if you try to emit a metric per token synchronously. we batch metric aggregation in-process and flush at short intervals. the kernel execution path is kept minimal — we do sampling and aggregated counters to avoid per-token syscalls.

[04:00] Mark Chen: Another thing to watch is exporter backpressure. if OTLP endpoint is slow you can buffer in the collector; on Dedicated we have quotas and backpressure heuristics to avoid request latency impact.

[04:18] Sofia Alvarez: talk to me about trace contexts. we want to correlate a user's frontend request through our API gateway, through Redwood, and back. how do you propagate trace ids?

[04:26] Liam O'Connor: we follow W3C Trace Context. Redwood includes the incoming traceparent and tracestate headers if present and continues the span tree. we add a redwood.request_id tag for easier joins. we also emit logs with trace id so you can join traces and logs in Grafana Loki or your log store.

[04:50] Gabe Turner: Are there any gotchas with load balancers or proxies in our VPC? we use nginx and an internal ALB.

[04:56] Priya Desai: make sure proxies forward the trace headers and don't sample them away. also check that your OTLP exporter can reach the collector — network egress rules in VPC are commonly the issue.

[05:18] Nadia Li: Sampling strategies — what do you recommend for production at scale?

[05:22] Priya Desai: multi-tiered sampling. by default: keep 100% of root spans for request-level metrics but sample child spans. use probabilistic sampling for traces (e.g., 0.1%-1% overall), and increase sampling rate for anomalous responses (errors, tail latency) using tail-sampling in the collector. we can show a config for tail-based sampling that retains traces with high kernel time or high token counts.

[05:50] Sofia Alvarez: tail-sampling seems key. does that affect memory on the collector?

[05:54] Liam O'Connor: yes collectors doing tail-sampling hold spans briefly (10-30s) so allocate memory accordingly. for very high qps you need horizontal scale or a policy that samples only on error/latency thresholds rather than per-token thresholds.

[06:12] Mark Chen: quick interjection — on quantization and batch size: quantized models change kernel timings and your per-token timing distribution. Batching reduces per-token overhead but increases tail latency for small latency-sensitive requests. we recommend recording batch_size histograms in metrics so you can correlate batch size vs latency.

[06:34] Gabe Turner: ok so metrics list to include: tokens_generated_total, tokens_per_request_histogram, batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_hits/misses, kernel_exec_time_seconds histogram, request_queue_time_seconds, and model_variant tag. anything else?

[06:48] Priya Desai: also include model_load_time_seconds for cold starts, quantization_profile label, and gpu_utilization_percent per node. we also surface memory pressure and swap events for on-prem.

[07:00] Sofia Alvarez: dashboards — do you have a starter Grafana dashboard we can import?

[07:04] Priya Desai: yes we'll send the JSON. it has panels for token throughput, p50/p90/p99 token latency, batch size heatmap, kv cache hit ratio, and traces linked to panels. link: https://redwood.example/dashboards/otel-token-metrics.json

[07:18] Nadia Li: how do we avoid high-cardinality tag explosion? model+tenant+region will create many series.

[07:24] Liam O'Connor: important to control cardinality: avoid free-form tags like request_id or user_id on metrics. use label cardinality limits and aggregate by tenant where possible. we recommend a metric tagging policy: keep model, region, and instance type; for tenant use tenant_id only for sampled traces, not metrics.

[07:46] Sofia Alvarez: what about token-level billing attribution? we need to tie tokens to customer/organization for cost reporting but without adding cardinality to metrics.

[07:55] Priya Desai: common pattern: emit metrics aggregated per-tenant on a separate low-cardinality bucketing (e.g., tenant tier or hashed bucket) and keep full per-tenant logs in an internal billing pipeline. or push per-request token counts to a billing service asynchronously (Kafka) rather than as high-cardinality Prometheus labels.

[08:20] Gabe Turner: Private deployment specifics — where should the collector live? sidecar vs agent vs central collector?

[08:27] Liam O'Connor: for Redwood Private we recommend a small footprint collector as a daemonset on each node to capture node-local metrics and push to your internal OTLP gateway. sidecars add overhead per pod; daemonset is more performant for high qps. for on-prem isolated environments you can run a central aggregator behind your firewall.

[08:48] Nadia Li: any recommendations for retention and storage? we use Prometheus Thanos for long term.

[08:54] Priya Desai: Prometheus + Thanos or Cortex is a good pattern. store metrics at 15-60s resolution long-term and keep high-resolution (5s) for 24-72h for incident triage. traces typically kept short unless sampled or stored in a trace-specific long-term store.

[09:14] Sofia Alvarez: security: will trace data or token counts ever include PII? how do we handle redaction?

[09:19] Mark Chen: we never include actual user prompt content in telemetry by default. only token counts/latency/aggregate stats are sent. if you want payload-level traces for debugging, we recommend an opt-in scrubber with PII redaction and storing those traces in a walled-off secure store with restricted access.

[09:40] Gabe Turner: that fits our compliance needs. send us the security docs.

[09:45] Priya Desai: noted — we'll include SOC2, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration notes for Private.

[09:52] Nadia Li: any real-world perf impact numbers for token-level metrics? roughs are fine.

[09:56] Priya Desai: anecdotal numbers: aggregated counters add <1% CPU overhead when batched; token-level synchronous emission can add 5-10% depending on model and qps. sampling traces at 0.1% is effectively negligible but gives rich spans. kv cache lookups are sub-ms usually but cache misses add a few ms to kernel exec time. we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet. link: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/token-metrics-24h.xlsx

[10:22] Mark Chen: demo time — Priya, can you walk through our otel-collector.yaml example and a sample Grafana dashboard?

[10:26] Priya Desai: sure — screen share; describing: collector receives OTLP and Prometheus scrape, does tail-sampling rules and routes metrics to your Prometheus remote write and traces to Jaeger/Tempo via OTLP. key snippet: tail-sampling rule that keeps traces with attributes: kernel_exec_time_seconds bucket > 0.2s OR kv_cache_miss=true OR http.status_code >= 500. (note: screen link omitted in transcription)

[11:05] Sofia Alvarez: nice. in the dashboard panel can we link traces to specific high kernel times?

[11:09] Priya Desai: yes panels have a trace link using trace_id. clicking opens trace in Tempo/Jaeger. we add a small action button that runs a filtered query for that request_id.

[11:28] Gabe Turner: any guidance on retention for token-count logs we push to Kafka for billing?

[11:32] Liam O'Connor: keep raw per-request token counts for 30-90 days depending on billing disputes SLA, then aggregate monthly. keep aggregated billing metrics indefinitely.

[11:45] Nadia Li: service accounts/keys for OTLP? how do we authenticate exporters to our collector in Private?

[11:50] Priya Desai: mutual TLS is our recommended approach; you can also use mTLS + token auth. we'll include examples for HashiCorp Vault and KMS for key rotation.

[12:06] Mark Chen: ok we're about 45 minutes in — quick recap and next steps?

[12:12] Sofia Alvarez: recap: we need the otel collector config, Grafana JSON, benchmark sheet, security docs, and Redwood will help with the 24h Dedicated run.

[12:20] Priya Desai: yep will send otel-collector.yaml, Grafana JSON, and the benchmark spreadsheet we referenced. we'll also include a short writeup on cardinality best practices and a sample billing pipeline pattern.

[12:31] Gabe Turner: i'll get our scrape config and retention details over.

[12:35] Nadia Li: schedule a follow-up 1:1 next week to kick off the Dedicated run.

[12:40] Mark Chen: awesome. thanks everyone — action items and dates in the notes. we'll follow up in email with links.

[12:48] End of call.

Notes/links referenced: https://redwood.example/docs/observability/otel-collector-sample, https://redwood.example/dashboards/otel-token-metrics.json, https://redwood.example/benchmarks/token-metrics-24h.xlsx
